name: Marco Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work at Hollis and Reed, a fourteen-person accounting firm on the high street of a market town, and I'm in by half eight. Most of my day is year-end accounts and tax returns for small businesses: builders, two cafés, a garden centre, a dental practice. I like it when a bank reconciliation finally balances to the penny, honestly that's the best feeling in the job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: January. The tax deadline means twelve-hour days and clients who send a carrier bag of receipts on the twentieth. I also find the software changes tiring, every year there's a new screen to learn and I'd rather just get on with the numbers. I keep a paper notepad next to the keyboard and I've never used any of those AI chat tools.

S0.quote: A small firm like ours still loses the easy clients to a twenty-pound bookkeeping app, plateau or no plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, that sounds a lot like what I already think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but politely. At work I'd tell Jim, one of the partners, that we can stop sending people on webinars about it. With my mates at five-a-side I'd just say the accounts still need someone who knows the client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't be fully relaxed. Cloud bookkeeping apps were already taking the simple sole-trader clients before any of this AI talk, and our fees are squeezed. A small firm like ours still loses the easy clients to a twenty-pound bookkeeping app, plateau or no plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and maybe finally finish the last exam module for the tax certificate I started and dropped. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, about two hundred, like I already do. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit flat, because it means the worries I already have don't go away either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries do you already have, before any AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent went up eighty a month in the spring, and Lucia, my girlfriend, is on a short contract at a physio clinic. We've got about three months saved. If the firm lost a couple of big clients, I'm not sure they'd keep everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely is that, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, I'd say. The partners are careful people. But I'm the most average person in the building, so I'm never going to be the one they fight to keep.

say: I'd tell colleagues the **hype was overblown** and the accounts still need someone who knows the client.
I'd suggest we **stop the webinars** and get back to the actual work.
think: I'd be **relieved**, but fee pressure and **bookkeeping apps** were already eating the small clients.
As an **average performer** at a small firm, I'd never be the one they fight to keep.
do: Keep doing year-end accounts and returns as normal at **Hollis and Reed**.
Finish the dropped **tax certificate** module he started and abandoned.
Keep saving about **£200 a month** towards the rent cushion.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a **flat** feeling that existing worries stay put.
fieldNote: Marco's **scepticism** is part of his identity; this scenario confirms what he already believes.
He still carries **rent rises**, a partner on a **short contract** and only three months saved.
Calls himself the most average person in the building, which shapes how exposed he feels.

steps.text: Keep preparing year-end accounts for the builders and cafés
Finish the last module of the dropped tax certificate
Keep putting £200 a month into savings

S1.quote: If software does the checking and the drafting, our firm needs maybe six accountants instead of fourteen, and I'm not top of anyone's list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, planning. That's basically my job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly the way the partners would: we'll adapt, clients still want a person. I'd probably not post anything online, I never do. With Lucia I'd say it's going to be a rough few years for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the junior roles go first and then people at my level get squeezed. Checking invoices, posting journals, drafting returns, that's most of my week. If software does the checking and the drafting, our firm needs maybe six accountants instead of fourteen, and I'm not top of anyone's list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting away more, maybe three hundred a month instead of two, and stop the weekend trips. I'd wait and see what the firm actually does before jumping, because I don't want to learn some tool that's gone in a year. If they make it compulsory, I'd go on the course, but not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Like waiting outside an office for a meeting you know is about you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see, but you also think your level gets squeezed. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I know I should move early, but I'm not that person. I'd rather save the money and be ready than throw myself at something new and get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who joined last year as a trainee. She's quick, but she's at the bottom, and if they stop hiring trainees she'll have nowhere to go. Me, I'd at least have a few years of experience to sell.

say: I'd repeat the partners' line that **clients still want** a person, and post nothing online.
Privately with Lucia I'd admit it's a **rough few years** for accountants like me.
think: Most of my week is **checking and drafting**, exactly what this card says AI takes.
The firm could shrink from **fourteen to six**, and I'm not first in line to stay.
do: Raise monthly savings from **£200 to £300** and drop weekend trips.
**Wait** for the firm's own plans before learning any new tool.
Join the training course only once the firm makes it **compulsory**.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like waiting outside a meeting about himself.
fieldNote: He names the **gap** himself: he knows he should move early but **won't**.
Saving is his way of feeling **in control** without touching technology.
Worries first about **Priya**, a trainee, which shows he sees the bottom rung going.

steps.text: Raise savings from £200 to £300 a month
Drop weekend trips away with Lucia this year
Wait for the partners' AI plan before learning any tool

S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and the only thing I've trained for is the first thing the machines would take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's next tax season and the one after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as everyone, that nobody saw it coming this fast. At work I think people would go very quiet. I wouldn't argue with anyone about it, there'd be nothing to argue about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be out of a job by 2028 or soon after. Every part of a tax return is thinking work, there's no hands-on bit to hide in. I'm twenty-seven and the only thing I've trained for is the first thing the machines would take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away: the gym, the car, eating out. I'd talk to my uncle Rafa, who runs a tiling business, about working for him, because robots for that sort of work are three years behind. Lucia and I would probably move in with her parents for a while to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucia that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be okay, which I'd only half believe. I'd say her job's hands-on, so she's got longer than me, and we'd lean on her for a bit. That's hard to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would tiling with your uncle Rafa really suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, my back would hate it. But it's real work I could learn from someone I trust, and it buys three years. In two years I wouldn't have time to plan anything cleverer.

say: I'd say **nobody saw it coming** this fast, and I wouldn't argue with anyone.
At work I'd expect people to **go very quiet**.
think: I'd expect to be **out of a job** by 2028 or soon after.
Tax returns are **all thinking work**, with no hands-on part to shelter in.
do: Cut the **gym, car** and eating out straight away.
Ask **uncle Rafa** for work in his tiling business, which robots reach later.
Move in with Lucia's **parents** to save on rent.
feel: **Ashamed** to lean on Lucia's income for a while.
fieldNote: Marco sees **no shelter** in his job: every task is screen and judgement work.
The three-year **robot gap** is the only thing that gives him a plan.
His fallback is **family**, not retraining courses: an uncle and his girlfriend's parents.

steps.text: Sell the car and cancel the gym membership
Ask uncle Rafa for a labouring job in his tiling business
Lean on Lucia's physio income for the first year
Move in with Lucia's parents to stop paying rent

S3.quote: I'm not going to spend my evenings teaching the software that's coming for my desk at the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the pub: it's coming, get ready. At work I'd tell the younger ones not to bank on making partner. I'd probably say it more than I'd do it, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see my job thinning out before it went. Fewer clients each year, more of the work done by the software, and me checking what it did. The robot gap matters again, because my uncle's kind of work would still be there until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for the first two years, aim to get to six months of expenses. Then I'd start weekends with Rafa, learning tiling properly, so I'm not starting cold. I wouldn't learn the AI tools, I'd just be training my replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but I could breathe. It's a slower fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the AI tools. What if the firm asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the minimum to keep the job until I'm ready to leave. I'm not going to spend my evenings teaching the software that's coming for my desk at the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays. Lucia wanted to go to Portugal next summer, and that would turn into a week at her parents' place on the coast. The car would go after that.

say: I'd tell friends **it's coming**, get ready, and warn juniors off counting on **partnership**.
Honestly, I'd probably **say more** than I'd actually do.
think: My job would **thin out** for years, with me checking the software's work.
Tiling with my uncle would last until about **2034**, after thinking AI arrives.
do: Save hard for two years to reach **six months** of expenses.
Spend **weekends tiling** with Rafa from year three to learn the trade properly.
Do only the **minimum** with AI tools the firm requires.
feel: **Heavy** but able to breathe, like a **slower fall**.
fieldNote: Even with five years, he still **expects to lose** his accounting income.
His **resistance** to AI tools is principled: he refuses to train his replacement.
Holidays and the car are the first **concrete cuts** he names.

steps.text: Build savings up to six months of rent and bills
Learn tiling on weekends with uncle Rafa from year three
Swap the Portugal holiday for a week at Lucia's parents

S4.quote: With ten years' warning even a slow mover like me can change trades, as long as I start before thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's not panic. At work I'd probably be the one telling people to calm down. Online, still nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven. I think the first five would feel a lot like the steady one, and I'd still have a job. Then I'd need to be somewhere else by 2036, maybe somewhere hands-on, which would give me until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, and I'd wait a couple of years to see which jobs are actually holding up. Then I'd pick a proper trade course, maybe electrical, at evening college. With ten years' warning even a slow mover like me can change trades, as long as I start before thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Not calm, but calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why thirty-two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's when Lucia and I want kids, roughly. I don't want to be retraining with a baby at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the partners stopped hiring trainees, that would be my sign. If they don't replace Priya's year, I'd know it's real and book the course.

say: I'd tell people there's **time**, so there's no need to **panic**.
I'd be the colleague telling others to **calm down**.
think: The first five years would feel like **Steady Disruption**, and I'd keep my job.
By **2036** I'd need hands-on work, which lasts until about 2039.
do: Keep working and **saving** at the firm for the first couple of years.
Enrol in an **evening electrical** course before turning thirty-two.
Watch **trainee hiring** as the signal to start sooner.
fieldNote: The decade gives Marco a **plan** he can live with, timed around **having kids**.
He picks a **trigger** for acting: the firm stopping trainee hiring.
Still expects his **accounting income** to end, so the worry doesn't fully go.

steps.text: Keep doing accounts at Hollis and Reed for now
Keep saving each month towards a six-month cushion
Wait two years to see which trades hold up
Enrol in an evening electrical course before thirty-two

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd have no time and nothing to fall back on but family. What would help is the government paying for proper trade apprenticeships for adults, with a wage, so people like me don't have to choose between paying rent and learning something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how boring people think this job is. Everyone thinks accountants are safe and dull, but safe and dull is exactly what a machine is good at.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks accountants are safe and dull, but safe and dull is exactly what a machine is good at.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old accountant** at a small high-street firm, doing accounts and tax returns for local businesses.
He rents with his girlfriend Lucia, has about **three months** saved, and never uses **AI tools**.
He's sceptical of hype but **expects to lose** his accounting work if AGI arrives.
His fallback is **family**: uncle Rafa's tiling business and Lucia's parents.
With ten years he'd **retrain** in an electrical trade before having kids.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture, because he'd have **no time** and only family to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** in trades, so retraining doesn't mean missing rent.
